"Implement the solution in parallel_letter_frequency.cpp, parallel_letter_frequency.h so that the tests in parallel_letter_frequency_test.cpp pass. The specification follows.

# Instructions

Count the frequency of letters in texts using parallel computation.

Parallelism is about doing things in parallel that can also be done sequentially.
A common example is counting the frequency of letters.
Employ parallelism to calculate the total frequency of each letter in a list of texts.


# Instructions append
 
## Additional Notes for C++ Implementation

There are several ways how to achieve parallelism in C++.
Exercism's online runner supports C++17, so you can use execution policies from the [algorithms library][algorithm].
Another option is manually managing [threads][thread].
However, note that spawning a thread is quite expensive (using a [thread pool][pool] would help).

When working locally, you can of course use whatever you want.
However, a solution using non-standard libraries will most probably not work with the Exercism online runner.

### Benchmark

When working locally, you can optionally run a benchmark to get an idea about the speedup of different implementations.
Activating the CMake flag `EXERCISM_INCLUDE_BENCHMARK` enables the benchmark:
```
cmake -DEXERCISM_RUN_ALL_TESTS=1 -DEXERCISM_INCLUDE_BENCHMARK=1 .
```

### Compiler support for parallel algorithms

GCC's implementation of the C++ standard library (`libstdc++`) relies on [TBB][tbb].
If TBB is not available, a fall back to a sequential version will be used, even when parallel execution is requested.

On Ubuntu, you need to install the `libtbb-dev` package:
```
apt-get install libtbb-dev
```

On macOS, you can use [Homebrew][homebrew] to install TBB:
```
brew install tbb
```

Clang `libc++` as of version 17 has experimental, partial support for parallel algorithms.
To switch it on, the `-fexperimental-library` compiler flags needs to be given.

Apple Clang 15 and earlier _do not_ support parallel algorithms.

On Linux and macOS we recommend using GCC (along with the default `libstdc++`) for this exercise.

Microsoft's MSVC supports parallel algorithms at least since VS 2017 15.7 without having to install any additional library.

[algorithm]: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm
[thread]: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/thread/thread
[pool]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thread_pool
[tbb]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threading_Building_Blocks
[homebrew]: https://brew.sh/


Do NOT modify the tests or the build files except as stated below. Do not create new files unless the specification requires them; Helper .h / .cpp files may go beside the solution."

237:         "advantageous for man and must always be a law for mankind? So far, "

245:         "that is, incessantly and eternally to make new roads, wherever\n"
246:         "they may lead. But the reason why he wants sometimes to go off at a "
247:         "tangent may just be that he is\n"
248:         "predestined to make the road, and perhaps, too, that however stupid "
249:         "the \"direct\"\n"
250:         "practical man may be, the thought sometimes will occur to him that "
251:         "the road almost always does lead\n"
252:         "somewhere, and that the destination it leads to is less important "
253:         "than the process\n"
254:         "of making it, and that the chief thing is to save the well-conducted "
255:         "child from despising engineering,\n"
256:         "and so giving way to the fatal idleness, which, as we all know,\n"
257:         "is the mother of all the vices. Man likes to make roads and to "
258:         "create, that is a fact beyond dispute.\n"
259:         "But why has he such a passionate love for destruction and chaos "
260:         "also?\n"
261:         "Tell me that! But on that point I want to say a couple of words "
262:         "myself. May it not be that he loves\n"
263:         "chaos and destruction (there can be no disputing that he does "
264:         "sometimes love it)\n"
265:         "because he is instinctively afraid of attaining his object and "
266:         "completing the edifice he is constructing?\n"
267:         "Who knows, perhaps he only loves that edifice from a distance, and is "
268:         "by no means\n"
269:         "in love with it at close quarters; perhaps he only loves building it "
270:         "and does not want to live in it,\n"
271:         "but will leave it, when completed, for the use of les animaux "
272:         "domestiques -\n"
273:         "such as the ants, the sheep, and so on. Now the ants have quite a "
274:         "different taste.\n"
275:         "They have a marvellous edifice of that pattern which endures for ever "
276:         "- the ant-heap.\n"
277:         "With the ant-heap the respectable race of ants began and with the "
278:         "ant-heap they will probably end,\n"
279:         "which does the greatest credit to their perseverance and good sense. "
280:         "But man is a frivolous and\n"
281:         "incongruous creature, and perhaps, like a chess player, loves the "
282:         "process of the game, not the end of it.\n"
283:         "And who knows (there is no saying with certainty), perhaps the only "
284:         "goal on earth\n"
285:         "to which mankind is striving lies in this incessant process of "
286:         "attaining, in other words,\n"
287:         "in life itself, and not in the thing to be attained, which must "
288:         "always be expressed as a formula,\n"
289:         "as positive as twice two makes four, and such positiveness is not "
290:         "life, gentlemen,\n"
291:         "but is the beginning of death.\n",
292: 
293:         "But these are all golden dreams. Oh, tell me, who was it first "
294:         "announced,\n"
295:         "who was it first proclaimed, that man only does nasty things because "
296:         "he does not know his own interests;\n"
297:         "and that if he were enlightened, if his eyes were opened to his real "
298:         "normal interests,\n"
299:         "man would at once cease to do nasty things, would at once become good "
300:         "and noble because,\n"
301:         "being enlightened and understanding his real advantage, he would see "
302:         "his own advantage in the\n"
303:         "good and nothing else, and we all know that not one man can, "
304:         "consciously, act against his own interests,\n"
305:         "consequently, so to say, through necessity, he would begin doing "
306:         "good? Oh, the babe! Oh, the pure,\n"
307:         "innocent child! Why, in the first place, when in all these thousands "
308:         "of years has there been a time\n"
309:         "when man has acted only from his own interest? What is to be done "
310:         "with the millions of facts that bear\n"
311:         "witness that men, consciously, that is fully understanding their real "
312:         "interests, have left them in the\n"
313:         "background and have rushed headlong on another path, to meet peril "
314:         "and danger,\n"
315:         "compelled to this course by nobody and by nothing, but, as it were, "
316:         "simply disliking the beaten track,\n"
317:         "and have obstinately, wilfully, struck out another difficult, absurd "
318:         "way, seeking it almost in the darkness.\n"
319:         "So, I suppose, this obstinacy and perversity were pleasanter to them "
320:         "than any advantage....\n"
321:         "Advantage! What is advantage? And will you take it upon yourself to "
322:         "define with perfect accuracy in what the\n"
323:         "advantage of man consists? And what if it so happens that a man's "
324:         "advantage, sometimes, not only may,\n"
325:         "but even must,  consist in his desiring in certain cases what is "
326:         "harmful to himself and not advantageous.\n"
327:         "And if so, if there can be such a case, the whole principle falls "
328:         "into dust. What do you think -\n"
329:         "are there such cases? You laugh; laugh away, gentlemen, but only "
330:         "answer me: have man's advantages been\n"
331:         "reckoned up with perfect certainty? Are there not some which not only "
332:         "have not been included but cannot\n"
333:         "possibly be included under any classification? You see, you gentlemen "
334:         "have, to the best of my knowledge,\n"
335:         "taken your whole register of human advantages from the averages of "
336:         "statistical figures and\n"
337:         "politico-economical formulas. Your advantages are prosperity, wealth, "
338:         "freedom, peace - and so on, and so on.\n"
339:         "So that the man who should, for instance, go openly and knowingly in "
340:         "opposition to all that list would to your thinking,\n"
341:         "and indeed mine, too, of course, be an obscurantist or an absolute "
342:         "madman: would not he? But, you know, this is\n"
343:         "what is surprising: why does it so happen that all these "
344:         "statisticians,  sages and lovers of humanity,\n"
345:         "when they reckon up human advantages invariably leave out one? They "
346:         "don't even take it into their reckoning\n"
347:         "in the form in which it should be taken, and the whole reckoning "
348:         "depends upon that. It would be no greater matter,\n"
349:         "they would simply have to take it, this advantage, and add it to the "
350:         "list. But the trouble is, that this strange\n"
351:         "advantage does not fall under any classification and is not in place "
352:         "in any list. I have a friend for instance ...\n"
353:         "Ech! gentlemen, but of course he is your friend, too; and indeed "
354:         "there is no one, no one to whom he is not a friend!\n",
355:         "Yes, but here I come to a stop! Gentlemen, you must excuse me for "
356:         "being over-philosophical;\n"
357:         "it's the result of forty years underground! Allow me to indulge my "
358:         "fancy. You see, gentlemen, reason is an excellent thing,\n"
359:         "there's no disputing that, but reason is nothing but reason and "
360:         "satisfies only the rational side of man's nature,\n"
361:         "while will is a manifestation of the whole life, that is, of the "
362:         "whole human life including reason and all the impulses.\n"
363:         "And although our life, in this manifestation of it, is often "
364:         "worthless, yet it is life and not simply extracting square roots.\n"
365:         "Here I, for instance, quite naturally want to live, in order to "
366:         "satisfy all my capacities for life, and not simply my capacity\n"
367:         "for reasoning, that is, not simply one twentieth of my capacity for "
368:         "life. What does reason know? Reason only knows what it has\n"
369:         "succeeded in learning (some things, perhaps, it will never learn; "
370:         "this is a poor comfort, but why not say so frankly?)\n"
371:         "and human nature acts as a whole, with everything that is in it, "
372:         "consciously or unconsciously, and, even it if goes wrong, it lives.\n"
373:         "I suspect, gentlemen, that you are looking at me with compassion; you "
374:         "tell me again that an enlightened and developed man,\n"
375:         "such, in short, as the future man will be, cannot consciously desire "
376:         "anything disadvantageous to himself, that that can be proved "
377:         "mathematically.\n"
378:         "I thoroughly agree, it can - by mathematics. But I repeat for the "
379:         "hundredth time, there is one case, one only, when man may "
380:         "consciously, purposely,\n"
381:         "desire what is injurious to himself, what is stupid, very stupid - "
382:         "simply in order to have the right to desire for himself even what is "
383:         "very stupid\n"
384:         "and not to be bound by an obligation to desire only what is sensible. "
385:         "Of course, this very stupid thing, this caprice of ours, may be in "
386:         "reality,\n"
387:         "gentlemen, more advantageous for us than anything else on earth, "
388:         "especially in certain cases. And in particular it may be more "
389:         "advantageous than\n"
390:         "any advantage even when it does us obvious harm, and contradicts the "
391:         "soundest conclusions of our reason concerning our advantage -\n"
392:         "for in any circumstances it preserves for us what is most precious "
393:         "and most important - that is, our personality, our individuality.\n"
394:         "Some, you see, maintain that this really is the most precious thing "
395:         "for mankind; choice can, of course, if it chooses, be in agreement\n"
396:         "with reason; and especially if this be not abused but kept within "
397:         "bounds. It is profitable and some- times even praiseworthy.\n"
398:         "But very often, and even most often, choice is utterly and stubbornly "
399:         "opposed to reason ... and ... and ... do you know that that,\n"
400:         "too, is profitable, sometimes even praiseworthy? Gentlemen, let us "
401:         "suppose that man is not stupid. (Indeed one cannot refuse to suppose "
402:         "that,\n"
403:         "if only from the one consideration, that, if man is stupid, then who "
404:         "is wise?) But if he is not stupid, he is monstrously ungrateful!\n"
405:         "Phenomenally ungrateful. In fact, I believe that the best definition "
406:         "of man is the ungrateful biped. But that is not all, that is not his "
407:         "worst defect;\n"
408:         "his worst defect is his perpetual moral obliquity, perpetual - from "
409:         "the days of the Flood to the Schleswig-Holstein period.\n",

## Summary

I implemented `parallel_letter_frequency::frequency` in the two solution files:

**`parallel_letter_frequency.h`** — declares the API:
```cpp
std::map<char, int> frequency(const std::vector<std::string_view>& texts);
```

**`parallel_letter_frequency.cpp`** — the implementation, which:
1. Returns an empty map immediately for empty input.
2. Spawns worker threads (`std::thread::hardware_concurrency()`, clamped to the number of texts so it never spawns more threads than there is work).
3. Partitions the texts into contiguous chunks, one per worker. Each worker counts letters into **its own** 26-entry `std::array<int, 26>`, so no two threads touch shared memory and no locking is needed.
4. Counts only alphabetic characters, case-insensitively (`std::tolower`), skipping whitespace/punctuation/digits. `char` is cast to `unsigned char` before `isalpha`/`tolower` to avoid undefined behavior for negative values.
5. Merges the per-worker tallies into the result map, skipping zero counts so letters that never appear don't show up (this is what makes the "ignore whitespace/punctuation/numbers" tests return an empty map).

I chose manual threads over `std::execution::par` because the exercise notes flag that Apple Clang's parallel-algorithm support is experimental and needs the `-fexperimental-library` flag — manual threads are portable and work with the default build.
